title: Tech futures slip as Nvidia earnings, Anthropic IPO and Warsh loom
dek: Nasdaq futures are pointing lower as the chip selloff that hit Wall Street on Friday spread through Asia overnight. Investors face a packed week: Fed Chair Warsh speaks at noon, Nvidia reports Tuesday and Anthropic's IPO is expected to price Wednesday, while markets are close to fully pricing a December rate hike.
quick: Nasdaq 100 futures were down about 1% and S&P 500 futures about 0.4% in early trading, according to Reuters; Dow futures were roughly flat.
Nvidia is down roughly 2% to 3.5% pre-market after its sixth straight weekly loss. It reports Tuesday after the close, its first report since Jensen Huang resigned as CEO.
Fed Chair Kevin Warsh speaks at noon ET. Fed funds futures put the odds of a December rate hike at roughly 90% or more.
Asia fell on chip stocks: the Nikkei lost 2.4% after Japan's economy unexpectedly shrank, and China's October data missed forecasts across the board.
Oil is holding near $96 Brent after Iran struck a US base in Bahrain on Sunday; gold touched its lowest level since October 2025 and Bitcoin hit a four-month low over the weekend.
Anthropic's IPO, at $70 to $78 a share, is expected to price Wednesday and start trading Thursday, according to reports.

blocks.head: Nvidia heads into its most closely watched report without Jensen Huang
blocks.what: Nvidia reports fiscal third-quarter results Tuesday after the close, its first since Huang resigned as CEO and longtime finance chief Colette Kress became interim CEO. Analysts expect earnings of about $2.48 a share on revenue of about $109.2 billion, against company guidance of roughly $108 billion. The stock fell 13% last week, its sixth straight weekly decline, closing Friday at $162.85, and its market value dropped below $4 trillion. Over the weekend, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent urged the company to pick an outside CEO, while two investors holding about $2.1 billion of stock asked the board to consider bringing Huang back, CNBC and the WSJ reported.
blocks.why: Nvidia is the largest weight in the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq, so its results and guidance move the whole index, chip suppliers in Asia, and AI-linked stocks from AMD and Broadcom to power and data-center names. Options markets are pricing a swing of roughly 8% in either direction after the report, according to options data cited by financial outlets.
blocks.watch: Leadership commentary on Tuesday's call, fiscal 2028 growth targets, China export rules, and any update on the board's CEO search.

blocks.head: Fed rate hike in December now close to fully priced
blocks.what: Hotter-than-expected October inflation data shifted rate expectations last week. Consumer prices rose 0.4% in October after 0.6% in September, and producer prices rose 0.3% on the month and 6.5% from a year earlier, with core producer prices up 0.5%, CNBC reported. CME FedWatch data cited by TheStreet put the chance of a quarter-point hike at the December 9 meeting at about 93%, and Saxo said futures price roughly 30 basis points of tightening for that meeting. Kansas City Fed President Jeffrey Schmid said Sunday that inflation is uncomfortably above the 2% target and moving the wrong way, though he did not call for more hikes.
blocks.why: Higher rate expectations keep Treasury yields above 5% on the 10-year, which weighs on high-valuation growth stocks, housing-related shares and non-yielding assets such as gold and crypto, and supports the dollar.
blocks.watch: Warsh's noon remarks, five other Fed speakers today, and Wednesday's FOMC minutes.

blocks.head: Anthropic's IPO, possibly the largest ever, is set for this week
blocks.what: Anthropic set a price range of $70 to $78 a share for 825 million shares, which would raise up to about $64.4 billion, according to its updated SEC filing. Seven tech companies, including Nvidia, are separately buying about $26 billion of stock in a private placement, bringing the total to as much as about $90 billion. Reports from CNBC and others say pricing is expected Wednesday and trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT on Thursday, though the company has not publicly confirmed the dates.
blocks.why: Demand for the deal is being read as a test of investor appetite for AI after a month-long selloff in AI stocks.
blocks.watch: Final pricing relative to the range, and first-day trading on Thursday.

blocks.head: Chip selloff spreads to Asia
blocks.what: Semiconductor stocks led Friday's US decline: AMD fell about 9%, Broadcom and Marvell each dropped close to 5%, and the Nasdaq lost 0.9% even as the Dow edged up. The selling carried into Asia on Monday, where Taiwan and South Korea led losses and SK Hynix fell more than 6%. Despite Friday's drop, all three major US indexes finished last week up more than 2%.
blocks.why: Tech is the largest sector in the S&P 500, so continued chip weakness pulls the index lower even when most other sectors rise, as happened Friday.
blocks.watch: Whether chip stocks stabilize before Nvidia's report.

blocks.head: Middle East: Iran strikes US base in Bahrain
blocks.what: Iran launched drone attacks on a US military base in Bahrain on Sunday, its second attack on Bahrain in days, according to CNBC, the NYT and the Guardian. Bahrain said it intercepted strikes. Brent crude briefly fell to about $94.30 before recovering to around $96.60, according to Saxo, as the International Energy Agency reported that global supply now exceeds demand.
blocks.why: Oil prices feed directly into inflation and therefore Fed expectations; energy stocks gained about 1% on Friday. So far, signs of oversupply have limited the price response to new attacks.
blocks.watch: Any disruption to Gulf shipping and whether Middle East talks are on the agenda at the APEC summit in Shenzhen on November 18 and 19, where China has confirmed plans for a meeting involving Xi, Trump and Putin.

blocks.head: Weak data from China and Japan
blocks.what: China's industrial output grew 4.8% from a year earlier in October, below the 5.3% expected in a Reuters poll, and retail sales rose only 0.4% against a 0.8% forecast. Fixed-asset investment fell 8.1% in January through October, with property investment down 21.6%. Japan's economy shrank at a 0.1% annualized rate in the third quarter, its first contraction in four quarters, versus forecasts for 0.3% growth, as higher energy costs weighed on consumers.
blocks.why: Slower growth in the world's second- and fourth-largest economies weighs on commodity demand, including copper, and on US multinationals that sell into Asia.

blocks.text: Asia

Japan's Nikkei 225 fell 2.4% to 59,662 as chip-related stocks such as Kioxia and Murata dropped more than 5% and the weak GDP report added pressure. Taiwan and South Korea led regional losses on the chip selloff. China's Shanghai Composite slipped 0.9% after the disappointing October data, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng bucked the trend with a gain of about 0.5%.
Europe

European stocks are little changed. The Stoxx 600 was near 665 in early trading, just above Friday's record close, with tech shares lagging ahead of Nvidia and miners down as copper hit a four-month low, according to Reuters. Germany's DAX and Britain's FTSE 100 were roughly flat to slightly higher.
Currencies

Currency moves were small as of the early-morning quotes. The dollar index was little changed near 103.5, holding up on expectations of a Fed hike. The euro was around $1.10 and the pound around $1.32, both slightly lower. The yen is weak, with the dollar near 159.5 yen, close to the 160 level, after Japan's GDP contraction. China's yuan was steady at about 6.67 per dollar.

US stock futures point to a lower open led by tech. Reuters reported Nasdaq 100 futures down about 1% and S&P 500 futures down about 0.4% in early trading, with Dow futures near flat. That repeats Friday's pattern, when the S&P 500 fell 0.4% to 7,561.67 and the Nasdaq fell 0.9% to 25,136.27 while the Dow rose 0.1% to 52,347.55.

The VIX volatility index ended Friday just above 20, a sign investors expect larger swings than usual this week. Options pricing cited by Saxo implies an S&P 500 move of about 0.9% today and about 1.8% through Friday, with Nvidia's report Tuesday as the main event.

Treasury yields eased slightly overnight after big increases last week. As of early-morning quotes, the 2-year yield was about 4.86%, the 10-year about 5.14% and the 30-year about 5.47%, each down 1 to 2 basis points. On Friday the 10-year rose about 4 basis points and touched 5.17% intraday after the producer price report, CNBC reported.

The curve is upward-sloping: the 10-year yields about 28 basis points more than the 2-year, and the 30-year about 33 basis points more than the 10-year. That means investors are still demanding extra pay for holding long-term bonds while they price a near-term hike.

Fed officials have been hawkish. Schmid of the Kansas City Fed said inflation is moving in the wrong direction. Governor Christopher Waller has left the door open to a larger half-point hike, according to market reports, though futures put the odds of that at about 10% or less. CME FedWatch data put the chance of a December hike at about 90% or more. Some strategists, including at TD Securities, said 10-year yields above 5% are worth buying on weakness, the WSJ reported.
Today's Fed speakers (ET)

items: Michael Barr, Fed governor: 5:00 a.m. (already spoken)
John Williams, New York Fed president: 9:05 a.m.
Kevin Warsh, Fed chair: 12:00 p.m., opening remarks at a Fed conference on productivity and jobs; markets want a signal on December
Beth Hammack, Cleveland Fed president: 2:15 p.m.

blocks.text: Friday's sector map showed a rotation away from tech. Technology was the worst S&P 500 sector, down about 2%, on the chip selloff. Consumer discretionary, industrials and materials also slipped. Defensive and value sectors led: consumer staples rose 1.4%, communication services about 1%, energy about 1% with oil, and financials 0.8%. Health care and utilities each gained about 0.5%.
That pattern of money moving from AI and chip stocks into staples, health care and banks has shown up repeatedly during the past month's AI selloff.
Pre-market movers

items: Nvidia: down roughly 2% to 3.5% in different pre-market readings, extending last week's 13% drop ahead of Tuesday's report and amid the debate over its next CEO.
Baidu: down about 1% pre-market after third-quarter results that Benzinga described as mixed against estimates.
Chipmakers broadly: AMD, Broadcom, Marvell and other semiconductor stocks are in focus after Friday's losses and the overnight selling in Taiwan and South Korea.

blocks.text: Oil

Brent was around $96 and US crude around $88 to $89 in early trading, roughly flat after swinging between losses and gains. Iran's attack on a US base in Bahrain adds supply risk, but reports from the IEA that global supply now exceeds demand for the first time since the war began have kept a lid on prices after a two-week slide.
Gold

Gold fell to about $3,832 an ounce in early Asian trading, its lowest since October 2025, before recovering to around $3,860. It lost about 4.5% last week. Rising yields and a firm dollar increase the cost of holding gold, which pays no interest, and that has outweighed demand for safety from the Middle East conflict.
Crypto

Bitcoin fell to a four-month low of about $62,080 on Sunday before recovering to around $64,500 to $65,000. Ether was around $1,800 after falling about 19.5% over the past week. US spot Bitcoin ETFs saw about $2.35 billion in outflows over two weeks, and a widely followed crypto sentiment gauge fell to 10, which is in the extreme fear range. Crypto has been trading with the AI and tech selloff and against rising rate expectations.
Today is light on economic data; Fed speakers are the main event.

items: Warsh at noon ET is the most important item. Any comments on inflation or the December meeting could move yields and the dollar.
Empire State manufacturing index, 8:30 a.m. ET: economists expect a reading near 17.6, down from 25.5 in October. It is still in expansion territory but a sign of cooling.
Williams (9:05 a.m.) and Hammack (2:15 p.m.): further guidance on how many officials favor a hike.
Cleveland Fed inflation expectations, around 9:48 a.m. ET: the prior reading was 3.3%.

rows: AI cloud growth versus the decline in ad revenue; shares slightly lower pre-market on mixed results
Beef and chicken margins and fiscal 2027 outlook; read on food prices for consumers
Food-service demand and contract wins; outlook for the new fiscal year
Infrastructure and data-center design backlog; government spending exposure

blocks.text: The week's heavyweight is Nvidia on Tuesday after the close. Big retailers follow: Home Depot Tuesday, Lowe's, TJX and Target Wednesday, and Walmart Thursday, all before the open.

Tuesday is the biggest day: October retail sales (economists expect 0.2% growth after 0.8%), Home Depot before the open and Nvidia after the close. Wednesday brings housing starts, earnings from Lowe's, TJX and Target, the expected pricing of Anthropic's IPO, and minutes from the last Fed meeting at 2 p.m. ET, which markets will read for how many officials favored a hike. Thursday has Walmart's results, which are widely watched as a read on household spending, weekly jobless claims (about 199,000 expected), the Philadelphia Fed survey, and Anthropic's expected trading debut. The APEC summit in Shenzhen runs Wednesday and Thursday. Friday closes the week with the final University of Michigan consumer sentiment reading (about 52 expected) and its inflation expectations figure, which was 4.3% last time. Many Fed officials, including Waller, Williams and Barr, speak throughout the week.

bottom_line: The morning is cautious and tech-led to the downside. Investors are positioning ahead of Nvidia's earnings and Anthropic's IPO while markets price a near-certain Fed hike in December, and yields, oil and the dollar are holding steady.
